etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English brethen (“to breathe, blow, exhale, odour”), derived from Middle English breth (“breath”). Eclipsed Middle English ethien and orðiæn, from Old English ēþian and orþian (“to breathe”); as well as Middle English anden, onden, from Old Norse anda (“to breathe”). More at breath.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To draw air into (inhale), and expel air from (exhale), the lungs in order to extract oxygen and excrete waste gases.
(intransitive) To take in needed gases and expel waste gases in a similar way.
(transitive) To inhale (a gas) to sustain life.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: I am in health, I breathe.

quote.citation: 1805, Walter Scott, “(please specify the page)”, in The Lay of the Last Minstrel: A Poem, London:  […]  [James Ballantyne] for Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, […], and A[rchibald] Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Breathes there a man with soul so dead?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To draw something into the lungs.
(intransitive) To expel air from the lungs, exhale.
(transitive) To exhale or expel (something) in the manner of breath.

quote.citation: 2012, Timothy Groves, The Book Of Creatures, →ISBN, page 85:
quote.text: Mountain Drakes breathe fire, Ice Drakes breathe ice, Swamp Drakes breathe acid, and Forest Drakes breathe lightning.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give an impression of, to exude.
To pass like breath; noiselessly or gently; to emanate; to blow gently.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: The air breathes upon us here most sweetly.

quote.citation: 1812–1818, Lord Byron, “(please specify |canto=I to IV)”, in Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage. A Romaunt, London: Printed for John Murray, […]; William Blackwood, Edinburgh; and John Cumming, Dublin; by Thomas Davison, […], →OCLC, (please specify the stanza number):
quote.text: There breathes a living fragrance from the shore.

definitions.definition: (chiefly Evangelical and Charismatic Christianity, with God as agent) To inspire (scripture).

quote.citation: 1850, John Howard Hinton, On the Divine Inspiration of the Scriptures. A lecture, etc, page 16:
quote.text: The affirmation before us, then, will be, "All scripture is divinely breathed."

quote.citation: 1917, J. C. Ferdinand Pittman, Bible Truths Illustrated: For the Use of Preachers, Teachers, Bible-school, Christian Endeavor, Temperance and Other Christian Workers, page 168:
quote.text: […]  that God, who breathed the Scriptures, "cannot lie,"  […]

quote.citation: 2010, Jay E. Adams, The Christian Counselor's Manual: The Practice of Nouthetic Counseling, Zondervan, →ISBN:
quote.text: Paul says that since God breathed the Scriptures, they are therefore useful; he did not put it the other way around (i.e., that they are useful, therefore inspired).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To exchange gases with the environment.
(intransitive, now rare) To rest; to stop and catch one's breath.

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, “lxiiij”, in Le Morte Darthur, book X:
quote.text: Thenne they lasshed to gyder many sad strokes / & tracyd and trauercyd now bakward / now sydelyng hurtlyng to gyders lyke two bores / & that same tyme they felle both grouelyng to the erthe / Thus they fought styll withoute ony reposynge two houres and neuer brethed(please add an English translation of this quotation)

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iv]:
quote.text: Well! breathe awhile, and then to it again!

definitions.definition: (transitive) To stop, to give (a horse) an opportunity to catch its breath.
(transitive) To exercise; to tire by brisk exercise.
(transitive, figurative) To passionately devote much of one's life to (an activity, etc.).
